extracted.intended_audience: healthcare and pharmaceutical communications professionals / corporate communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for communications professionals in the healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors on ethical, accurate, and responsible messaging after the Theranos scandal; covers corporate, media, medical, investor, and board communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent and honest communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The scandal shed a light on the need for transparent and honest communication to help patients make informed health decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators should prioritize clear, evidence-based messaging so patients can make informed decisions; avoid ambiguity that could mislead about clinical benefits or safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize patient welfare over financial gain
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States versus Elizabeth Holmes trial highlights the fate of companies that focus on the dollar sign and not the patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications strategy should center patient safety and outcomes rather than promotional or investment-focused narratives that risk overstating impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate clinical efficacy; avoid unsubstantiated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies have put a greater emphasis on demonstrating clinical efficacy while staying away from making sweeping statements about their potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All public claims must be supported by scientific evidence; avoid broad or hyperbolic statements about potential impact without clinical validation. Example anti-pattern: investor decks and ads citing unsubstantiated claims with little-to-no scientific backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invest in PR before product validation
rubrics_metrics.description: From the founding of Theranos, Elizabeth poured money into PR before she even had a working product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy promotional activity or media narratives that pre-empt product validation; ensure product and data are credible before large-scale PR spend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic skepticism and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Theranos gave reporters yet another example of the value of skepticism. Journalists have a duty to share the truth and Theranos gave them a stark reminder of how cautious they must be – even when speaking with a lauded CEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For media-facing guidance: expect reporters to verify claims and be prepared to provide substantiating documentation. For journalists: corroborate high-profile claims, record and retain notes/interviews, and treat access to a CEO as insufficient proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using third‑party media coverage as proof of validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elizabeth used the Fortune spotlight to mislead the public as some kind of proof for her claims and misleading statements that she later shared with investors once the article was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat favorable press or profiles as substitute for scientific validation; companies and spokespeople should not present media coverage as evidence of efficacy or endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous MLR review for corporate messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Theranos’ messaging ... were riddled with misleading language and outlandish claims. ... boosting the importance of running all corporate messaging through rigorous MLR review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All clinical, regulatory, and promotional communications must pass medical, legal, and regulatory review to ensure accuracy, compliance, and appropriate evidence presentation. Be especially vigilant when communicating clinical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and cautious investor communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Holmes used her investor calls to hint at partnerships with the Department of Defense, suggest the Edison could perform 200 tests, and imply that Edison was validated by the ten largest pharmaceutical companies in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investor-facing statements must avoid insinuations of unconfirmed partnerships, overstatement of capabilities, or implying validation by third parties. Be explicit about what has been validated and what remains speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition should include medical expertise and be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: As members of a medical advisory board offer credibility and guidance, it is vital to share such selections with patients and investors, as it demonstrates measures taken to ensure patient safety and financial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure boards/advisory groups include relevant scientific/medical expertise and transparently disclose those appointments to demonstrate commitment to safety and credibility. Avoid relying solely on celebrity or political figures without domain expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate openly with all healthcare stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: We not only have an opportunity – but a responsibility – to communicate openly with patients, doctors, healthcare providers, partners and investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an open, evidence-based communication posture across audiences (patients, clinicians, partners, investors). Proactively share validated data, limitations, and steps taken to protect patient safety and ensure product reliability.
